content: Cervical polyps are benign, polypoid overgrowths of endocervical tissue. These growths typically project into the cervical canal and may protrude into the external cervix. The exact cause of cervical polyps remains unknown, but they are thought to arise due to chronic inflammation of the endocervical canal, hormonal factors, or vascular obstruction. They are more commonly observed in perimenopausal and postmenopausal women, with a prevalence of 5–10% in the general population. Cervical polyps can be classified based on their location. Ectocervical polyps originate from the outer surface layer of the cervix and are more common in postmenopausal women. Endocervical polyps, which develop from cervical glands within the cervical canal, are the most common type and are more frequently seen in premenopausal women. The pathogenesis of cervical polyps is characterized by chronic inflammation of the endocervical canal. Although the exact mechanism is unclear, contributing factors may include an abnormal response to elevated estrogen levels, chronic inflammation, or vascular obstruction. Gross pathology typically reveals a flesh-colored, finger-like growth measuring approximately 1 cm. Microscopic examination often shows inflamed and dilated endocervical glands surrounded by myxoid stroma. Cervical polyps are often asymptomatic, but when symptoms occur, they may include abnormal vaginal bleeding (intermenstrual or postcoital), vaginal discharge, dyspareunia, or dysmenorrhea. Diagnosis is typically made via cervical biopsy, which may reveal squamous metaplasia and inflammatory cells. Imaging, particularly ultrasound, can identify sessile or pedunculated masses within the endocervical canal, often with a visible stalk attaching the polyp to the cervical wall. Treatment of cervical polyps primarily involves surgical excision, often performed using ring forceps in conjunction with biopsy. Other surgical options include laser therapy or cauterization. If infection is present, antibiotics may be prescribed. There is no established medical therapy for cervical polyps. The prognosis for cervical polyps is excellent, with a 5-year survival rate of nearly 100%. However, approximately 7% of cases may progress to malignant transformation. Regular follow-up, including pelvic examinations, vaginal ultrasounds, and colposcopy, is recommended every 6 to 12 months after treatment to monitor for recurrence or complications. Preventive measures include periodic cervical screening and ultrasound evaluations. Early detection and treatment are key to preventing complications such as bleeding, recurrence, or malignant transformation.
